'''''Elodea canadensis''''' ('''American waterweed''' or '''Canadian waterweed''' or '''pondweed''') is a [[perennial]] [[aquatic plant]], or submergent [[macrophyte]], native to most of [[North America]].<ref name="fna">Flora of North America: [http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=220004673 ''Elodea canadensis'']</ref><ref name="bc">Plants of British Columbia: [http://linnet.geog.ubc.ca/Atlas/Atlas.aspx?sciname=Elodea+canadensis ''Elodea canadensis''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200809050853/http://linnet.geog.ubc.ca/Atlas/Atlas.aspx?sciname=Elodea+canadensis |date=2020-08-09 }}</ref><ref name="jeps">Jepson Flora: [http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?Elodea+canadensis ''Elodea canadensis'']</ref> It has been [[Introduced species|introduced]] widely to regions outside its native range.

==Distribution==
The native range of the species includes most of North America, from [[British Columbia]] east to [[Nova Scotia]], south to [[California]], and southeast to northern [[Florida]], in rivers and lakes from sea level up to {{cvt|2000|m}} altitude, primarily in lime-rich waters.<ref name="fna"/>

==Description==
Young plants initially start with a seedling stem with roots growing in mud at the bottom of the water; further adventitious roots are produced at intervals along the stem, which may hang free in the water or anchor into the bottom. It grows indefinitely at the stem tips, and single specimens may reach lengths of {{cvt|3|m}} or more.

The [[leaf|leaves]] are bright green, translucent, oblong, 6–17 mm long and 1–4 mm broad, borne in whorls of three (rarely two or four) round the stem.<ref name="The Wild Flower Key">{{cite book |last=Rose |first=Francis|author-link=Francis Rose  |title=The Wild Flower Key |year=2006 |publisher=Frederick Warne & Co|isbn=978-0-7232-5175-0 |pages=485–486}}</ref> It lives entirely underwater, the only exception being the small white or pale purple [[flower]]s which float at the surface and are attached to the plant by delicate stalks. These stalks, or [[hypanthium|hypanthia]], are the lower part of the petals joined to form a [[floral tube]]. This floral tube can be up to {{cvt|30|cm}} in length, while only 1 mm in width,<ref>{{cite book |  editor-last= Bailey | editor-first= Liberty Hyde | date= 1935 | title= Cyclopedia of Horticulture | location= New York | publisher= MacMillan and Co. | page= Vol. 1 p. 1110 }}</ref> for a length to width ratio of 300 fold.  However, according to one article, this ratio can sometimes be as much as one thousandfold.<ref>{{ cite journal | last= Wilie | first= Robert B. | date= January 1904 |title=The Morphology of Elodea canadensis | journal= Botanical Gazette | volume= 37 | issue= 1 | page= 4 }}</ref>

It is [[plant sexuality|dioecious]], with male and female flowers on different plants. The flowers have three small white petals; male flowers have 4.5–5 mm petals and nine [[stamens]], female flowers have 2–3 mm petals and three fused [[carpel]]s. The [[fruit]] is an ovoid [[capsule (fruit)|capsule]], about 6 mm long containing several [[seed]]s that ripen underwater. The seeds are 4–5 mm long, spindle-shaped and smooth.  It flowers from May to October.<ref name="fna" /><ref name="bc" /><ref name="jeps" /><ref name="rhs">Huxley, A., ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. Macmillan {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}.</ref>

It grows rapidly in favorable conditions and can choke shallow ponds, canals, and the margins of some slow-flowing rivers. It requires summer water temperatures of 10–25 °C and moderate-to-bright light levels.<ref name="rhs" />

It is closely related to ''[[Elodea nuttallii]]'', which generally has narrower leaves under 2 mm broad. It is usually fairly easy to distinguish from its relatives, like the Brazilian ''[[Egeria densa]]'' and ''[[Hydrilla|Hydrilla verticillata]]''. These all have leaves in whorls around the [[Plant stem|stem]]; however, ''Elodea'' usually has three leaves per whorl, whereas ''Egeria'' and ''Hydrilla'' usually have four or more. ''Egeria densa'' is also a larger, bushier plant, with longer leaves.<ref name="nfp">Native Freshwater Plants: [http://www.ecy.wa.gov/programs/wq/plants/native/elodea.html American Waterweed] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050613080232/http://www.ecy.wa.gov/programs/wq/plants/native/elodea.html |date=2005-06-13 }}</ref>

== Cultivation and uses ==
It is frequently used as an [[aquarium]] plant. Propagation is by cuttings.<ref name="hiscock">Hiscock, P. (2003). ''Encyclopedia of Aquarium Plants'' Interpret Publishing, United States and Canada {{ISBN|0-7641-5521-0}}.</ref>

==As an invasive species==
It is an [[invasive species]] in [[Europe]], [[Asia]], [[Africa]], and [[Oceania]]. Europe has been particularly affected, with the first records dating back as far as 1836 in [[County Down]], Ireland, and in [[Great Britain]] in 1841;<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Simpson|first=D.A.|date=1984|title=A short history on the introduction and spread of Elodea Michx. in the British Isles|journal=Watsonia|volume=15|pages=1–9}}</ref><ref>Hackney, P. 1992.(Ed.) Stewart and Corry's Flora of the North-east of [[Ireland]]. Institute of Irish Studies and The Queen's University of Belfast. {{ISBN|0-85389-446-9}} (HB)</ref> it is now abundant in both Ireland and Great Britain.<ref name="o841">{{cite web | title=Canadian Waterweed ''Elodea canadensis'' Michx. | website=PlantAtlas | url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.vea | access-date=2025-06-18}}</ref> The species' presence has been confirmed in all continental European countries,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Poulis|first1=Georgios|last2=Zervas|first2=Dimitrios|date=2017-12-20|title=First confirmed record of Elodea canadensis Michx. (Hydrocharitaceae) in Greece|journal=Hacquetia|language=en|volume=16|issue=2|pages=175–179|doi=10.1515/hacq-2017-0001|issn=1854-9829|doi-access=free|bibcode=2017Hacq...16..175P }}</ref> spreading through ponds, ditches and streams, which were often choked with its rank growth.<ref name="EB1911">{{EB1911|inline=y|wstitle=Water-thyme|volume=1|page=410}}</ref><ref name="rhs" /><ref name="nfp" />
